series.name: Story Stock
series.tagline: The promise was a multibagger. The autopsy says otherwise.
series.concept: 25-episode autopsy of Indian companies that were once 'the next big thing.' Mostly failures, occasional survivors. Pattern recognition over prediction. Each episode walks through one company a retail investor could plausibly have bought into, surfaces the visible warning signs that existed before the crash, and abstracts a transferable lesson. Five wins are scattered through the season to show what real compounding looks like when nobody is hyping it.

episodes.title: Manpasand Beverages

slides.text:
India's Coca-Cola for the small town.

Mango Sip in 200ml packs.
Railway-platform distribution.
Saif Ali Khan on every billboard.

₹140 in June 2015.
₹500 by April 2018.

Brokers called it a five-year ten-bagger.
The Hindi belt was just the beginning.

May 2018.

Deloitte Haskins & Sells resigned as auditor.

The reason given was four lines long.
The reason given was nothing.

Stock fell 20% the next day.

A year later, the promoter was arrested by GST officers.

The investigation surfaced inflated revenue, fake distributors, and circular sales.

Delisted from BSE in 2024.
Final price: ₹3.

STATUS: −99% from peak.
When an auditor resigns and won't say why, the four-line letter is the most expensive paragraph in finance.

Three things you can check, free, on the BSE site:

1. Auditor resignation without explanation
2. Sudden change of audit firm
3. Qualified opinion in any past auditor's report

One is a yellow card.
Two is a stop.
Three is an exit.

Next time on Story Stock:

A tech company whose stock ran 30% in a single day.

Every Friday.
For two years.

Until SEBI noticed.

episodes.synopsis: India's small-town Coca-Cola. Listed 2015 at ₹140; ran to ₹500 by early 2018. Saif Ali Khan brand ambassador. Then in May 2018 Deloitte resigned as auditor with a four-line letter and no reason. Stock dropped 20% the next day. A year later the GST department arrested the promoter. The investigation surfaced inflated revenue, fake distributors, and circular sales. Delisted from BSE in 2024. ₹500 to ₹3.
episodes.caption:
A juice company became India's hottest small-cap. Then the auditor walked out. Four lines, no reason. Stock fell 99%.

Which company were you watching when things got quiet?

episodes.title: Vakrangee
episodes.synopsis: Tech-services company running e-commerce + Aadhaar enrolment kiosks. 2017–18: stock ran from ₹150 to ₹500 in 14 months on parabolic single-day moves. Promoter pledging crossed 50%. SEBI's interim order in April 2018 alleged price manipulation. Stock fell 70% in eight sessions.

episodes.title: Bajaj Finance
episodes.synopsis: Small NBFC subsidiary in 2008. ₹50, no glamour. Branch expansion + credit-cycle discipline + cross-sell built a quiet compounder. ₹50 → ₹7,500+ in 14 years. Nobody on TV called it sexy until it had already done 50x.

episodes.title: PC Jeweller
episodes.synopsis: 2018 darling. Stock ran on news of new geographies and gold-loan deals. Receivables ballooned faster than revenue. Promoter pledging crept up. Buyback announcement was withdrawn. Stock fell 85% in a year.

episodes.title: Eros International
episodes.synopsis: Bollywood listed-co. Reported revenue grew while operating cash flow turned negative. Auditors flagged related-party concerns multiple years. Bonds in default. Stock down 99% from peak.

episodes.title: Cafe Coffee Day
episodes.synopsis: VG Siddhartha built a cafe empire and a tech-investing portfolio funded by pledging shares. Sale of Mindtree stake forced. Founder's note in 2019 referenced lender pressure. Stock collapsed.

episodes.title: Cox & Kings
episodes.synopsis: 250-year-old travel brand. 2019: defaulted on commercial paper. Forensic audit later surfaced approximately ₹3,000 crore of borrowings allegedly hidden through subsidiaries.

episodes.title: Eicher Motors
episodes.synopsis: 2008: a sleepy commercial-vehicle company with a forgotten motorbike brand called Royal Enfield. Siddhartha Lal bet on premiumization. ₹500 → ₹35,000 in 14 years.

episodes.title: Suzlon Energy
episodes.synopsis: Wind-energy poster child of the 2007 boom. Acquired REpower (Germany) on dollar debt. Sector slowed; rupee weakened; debt servicing ate everything. CDR, then default, then dilution. ₹460 to ₹6.

episodes.title: DHFL
episodes.synopsis: Housing-finance company. Cobrapost report and forensic audit alleged approximately ₹31,000 crore of related-party transactions. Wadhawan brothers arrested. IBC. Bondholders, mutual-fund holders, retail — all hit.

episodes.title: Educomp Solutions
episodes.synopsis: Pioneered 'Smart Class' in government schools. Revenue concentrated in state-government tenders that took 18+ months to pay. When working capital cracked, debt did too. Stock down 99%.

episodes.title: Yes Bank
episodes.synopsis: Aggressive corporate banking. Reported NPAs significantly diverged from RBI's audit findings (the 'asset quality divergence' disclosures). Rana Kapoor's exit. Moratorium March 2020. Restructured.

episodes.title: Page Industries
episodes.synopsis: Genomal family bought the Indian licence for Jockey in 1994. Listed in 2007 at ₹360. Distribution discipline + premium pricing + rising-income tailwind. ₹360 → ₹50,000+ at peak.

episodes.title: Vodafone Idea
episodes.synopsis: Merger of Vodafone India + Idea Cellular in 2018. AGR Supreme Court ruling in October 2019 retroactively imposed approximately ₹58,000 crore of dues. Capex needs + interest + AGR = unsustainable. Stock at single digits.

episodes.title: Future Retail
episodes.synopsis: Big Bazaar's parent. Kishore Biyani's acquisition spree leveraged the group across multiple listed entities. COVID-19 exposed the leverage. Reliance deal collapsed under Amazon's arbitration injunction. Liquidation.

episodes.title: Stayzilla
episodes.synopsis: Homestay marketplace. Founder publicly accused a vendor of extortion in 2017 and was arrested. The post outlived the company.

episodes.title: BYJU'S
episodes.synopsis: $22B unicorn at peak. Aggressive revenue recognition (annual subscriptions booked upfront), debt-funded acquisitions (Aakash, WhiteHat Jr, Epic), governance turnover, lender lawsuits, ED raids. Valuation cut by 99%+ in private markets.

episodes.title: Symphony
episodes.synopsis: Air coolers. Asset-light, dominant in domestic market, exported to hot countries. ₹3 in 2003 to ₹2,500 at peak.

episodes.title: Zilingo
episodes.synopsis: Singapore-based, India-built fashion-tech. CEO Ankiti Bose suspended in 2022 over alleged accounting irregularities. Founder–board war went public. Liquidation.

episodes.title: Satyam Computer Services
episodes.synopsis: January 2009. Founder Ramalinga Raju confessed in writing to fabricating approximately ₹7,000 crore of cash and revenue over years. The granddaddy of Indian accounting frauds.

episodes.title: Reliance Communications
episodes.synopsis: Anil Ambani's flagship. Telecom capex without commensurate ARPU. Dollar debt + Jio's entry + Ericsson default. Personal guarantees. IBC.

episodes.title: Jet Airways
episodes.synopsis: India's largest private airline. Fuel-price spike + low-cost competition + leverage + working-capital squeeze. Grounded April 2019.

episodes.title: Avanti Feeds
episodes.synopsis: Andhra Pradesh-based shrimp-feed company. Rode India's shrimp-export tailwind. ₹2 in 2009 to ₹2,000+ at peak.

episodes.title: Kingfisher Airlines
episodes.synopsis: Vijay Mallya's airline. Loss-making from inception. Funded by group cross-borrowing and bank loans. Never profitable. AOC suspended 2012. Mallya in London since 2016.

episodes.title: The Pattern
episodes.synopsis: Synthesis of the previous twenty-four episodes. Seven red flags that recurred across the failures: (1) auditor resignation or change without explanation; (2) promoter pledging above 40%; (3) operating cash flow that doesn't match reported revenue for 3+ years; (4) customer or geographic concentration above 50%; (5) acquisition spree funded by debt during a sector boom; (6) receivables growing faster than revenue; (7) public conflict between founder and board, regulator, or supply chain. Any one is a yellow card. Any two is a stop. Any three is an exit.
